To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
breast-milk Pb, HHg, and ethylmercury were significantly associated with poorer neurodevelopment at 24 months in children exposed to multiple neurotoxic metals.

(1) breast-milk Pb was negatively associated with Bayley MDI and with milestone achievement (walking age) at 24 months and (2) HHg was negatively associated with milestone achievement (talking age) at 6 months of age.
breast-milk Pb concentrations and HHg concentrations in children's hair were significantly higher in TOKS children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of multiple exposure to neurodevelopmental toxicants on children's neurodevelopment.

the potential neurodevelopmental impact of the perinatal multiple exposure of children from two communities in Brazil to neurotoxic substances, such as lead, mercury (ethyl and methyl forms), and aluminum.
the effects of perinatal exposure to a mixture of neurotoxic substances, which included lead, methylmercury (MeHg), and ethylmercury in the case of Thimerosal-containing vaccine (TCV).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of the multiple exposures of the infants in the present study to neurotoxic metals (Pb, Hg, ethylmercuy and Al) were not additive, but that they were synergistic.

the combined effect of multiple exposures to neurotoxic substances during pregnancy and lactation, including ethylmercury from TCV, may have a negative effect on neurodevelopment in children from the first 2 years of life, particularly in those with higher exposures.
the combined exposure to Pb and HHg in utero and postnatally was associated with lower MDI at 24 months.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
breast-milk Pb is a risk factor for neurodevelopment and that ethylmercury is a risk factor in the achievement of milestones.
breast-milk Pb exposure was a risk factor for neurodevelopmental delay at six and 18 months of age, whereas HHg and TCV ethylmercury were risk factors for neurodevelopmental delays at 24 months.
perinatal exposure to multiple neurotoxic substances may have a negative impact on neurodevelopment in infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combined exposure to multiple toxic metals (lead and methylmercury) and ethylmercury in breast-fed infants is associated with neurodevelopmental delays.
multiple exposures to neurotoxic substances in the first two years of life may be associated with neurodevelopmental deficits.
the neurodevelopment of infants from the two communities studied was affected by the multiple exposure to neurodevelopmental toxins.
